source_note: Goldner, 'A Markov Model of Football: Using Stochastic Processes to Model a Football Drive', Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports 2012, Manuscript 1400 (Keith Goldner, Northwestern University), DOI 10.1515/1559-0410.1400, 18 pages. A foundational absorbing-Markov drive model: state=(down,distance,yardline), 340 transient + 9 absorbing states (349 total) calibrated on 2005-2009 PBP (~200k plays/30k drives/1280 games), field binned into 20 five-yard zones and distance into 5-yard increments. Transition matrix partitioned Q/R/0/I; absorption probabilities B=(I-Q)^-1 R; expected absorption time t=(I-Q)^-1 c; expected points EP=rho_TD*7+rho_FG*3+rho_SAF*(-2)=B x A (TD valued 6.96 for 96% XP); Net Expected Points (NEP) = EP delta + points scored. Validated against actual drive endings with candid distance-binning bias (3rd-and-1 grouped with 3rd-and-5 underpredicts TD 37.9% vs 45.1%). Applied to 2010 team NEP (Eagles rushing +55.81 via Vick; run/pass on common EP scale). Extracted faithfully (not a derivative summary). Equations 1 (Markov property), 5 (absorption), 6 (expected time), 7 (EP) and the Q/R/0/I partition are printed as readable text math (not shifted-font) and rendered in labeled LaTeX. Domain football matches catalog; American football. The absorbing-chain drive model, absorption-probability and expected-points formulas, NEP play-value metric, distance-binning granularity tradeoff, and play-call non-Markovian caveat are directly isomorphic to GSE's drive-state, expected-points, and EPA layer. No sportsbook lines/spreads/totals/implied odds in source or lifted into GSE.

assumptions: Each drive has a finite number of states defined by down (1-4), distance to a first down (1-100), and yard line (1-99); a drive ends in a finite number of ways (scoring, giving the ball back, end of half/game), and the model estimates the probability of each ending from any situation.

primitives.name: Markov property: next state depends only on current state
primitives.verbatim_quote: The essence of a Markov chain is that the next state depends only on the current state

symbol_and_unit_ledger.X_n: drive state at play n (down, distance, yardline)

assumptions: The Markov property (Eq 1) states P(X_{n+1}=x | X_1=x_1,...,X_n=x_n) = P(X_{n+1}=x | X_n=x_n): the next state depends only on the current state, all previous events having no effect; a discrete-time finite-state chain where each step is a play. Equation 1 is printed as readable text math and used directly.

primitives.name: Caveat: prior play-calls affect future via game theory (run sets up play-action)

primitives.name: Drive = absorbing Markov chain; drive-endings are absorbing states
primitives.verbatim_quote: A football drive can be seen as an absorbing Markov chain
assumptions: A football drive is an absorbing Markov chain: as the number of plays goes to infinity the probability of ending in an absorbing state goes to 1, and it is impossible to leave an absorbing state (once a touchdown is scored the drive ends and the chain is absorbed); the drive-endings are the absorbing states.

layer2.mapping: The absorbing-chain drive framing is literally GSE's drive-as-absorbing-process model.
layer2.telemetry: absorbing Markov chain; P(absorbed)->1 as plays->inf; cannot leave absorbing state

primitives.name: Transition matrix partitioned Q (transient), R, 0, I (absorbing)
primitives.verbatim_quote: The whole transition matrix has n + r rows and columns, but can be divided into these four sub-matrices: Q, R, 0, I
primitives.latex: P=\begin{pmatrix}Q & R\\ 0 & I\end{pmatrix},\quad Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},\ R\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}
assumptions: The 349x349 transition matrix is partitioned (Grinstead 1997) into Q (n x n transient-to-transient), R (n x r transient-to-absorbing), 0 (r x n, cannot start absorbing), and I (r x r identity, cannot leave absorbing); the first 340 columns of the last 9 rows are 0 and the last 9 columns of the last 9 rows are 0 except a diagonal of 1s. reasoning_traces.think: The retrocausal genealogy of this paper is the founding of the absorbing-Markov drive model that underlies modern expected points. Keith Goldner, at Northwestern University, publishing in the Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports in 2012 as Manuscript 1400, builds on the expected-points lineage that began with Virgil Carter's Operations Research work for the Cincinnati Bengals in 1971, was refined in The Hidden Game of Football by Carroll and collaborators in 1989, and was advanced by Brian Burke, Aaron Schatz, and Ben Alamar after the recognition that field position and expected points are not linearly related. The motivating anecdote is the 2003 playoff fourth-and-twenty-six from the Eagles' own twenty-five, down three to Green Bay with seventy-two seconds left, which Donovan McNabb converted on a slant to Freddie Mitchell; the model assigns a drive containing that situation only a one-in-one-hundred-seventy-five chance of ending in a field goal. The recursive theory of mind is the absorbing Markov chain itself. A state is defined by down, distance to a first down, and yard line, and the Markov property says the next state depends only on the current one; the author explicitly qualifies that prior play-calls can affect the future through game theory, such as running to set up play-action, but since run and pass are not model variables the chain remains Markov in down-distance-yardline. The field is binned into twenty five-yard zones and distance into five-yard increments, with everything beyond twenty yards lumped, yielding three hundred forty transient states plus nine absorbing states — touchdown, field goal, safety, missed field goal, fumble, interception, turnover on downs, punt, and end of half or game — for three hundred forty-nine total, calibrated on roughly two hundred thousand plays across the 2005 to 2009 seasons. Cross-layer veto adjudication is the matrix algebra and its honest accuracy limits. The transition matrix is partitioned into Q, R, zero, and I; absorption probabilities are B equals the inverse of I minus Q times R; expected plays to absorption are t equals the inverse of I minus Q times the ones vector; and expected points are the absorption probabilities weighted by scoring values, EP equals rho-touchdown times seven plus rho-field-goal times three plus rho-safety times minus two, or in matrix form B times the value vector A, with the touchdown actually valued at six point nine six to reflect the ninety-six percent extra-point make rate. The validation is candid: a first-and-ten from the own twenty predicts field goals at nine point three percent versus ten point three actual, but the third-and-one state, grouped with third-and-five for frequency, underpredicts touchdowns at thirty-seven point nine percent versus forty-five point one actual, a seven-point-two gap that the author attributes to coarse distance binning and recommends correcting. The implementation invariants map directly onto GSE. The down-distance-yardline state is GSE's drive-state representation; the absorbing chain is GSE's drive-as-process model; the absorption-probability formula is GSE's drive-outcome computation; the expected-points formula is GSE's state value; and Net Expected Points, the difference in expected points across a play plus points scored, is GSE's EPA-style play value. The expected-absorption-time formula is GSE's drive-length estimate, and the common-scale run-versus-pass comparison is GSE's opportunity-cost baseline recognizing that passing is generally more efficient. The outputs are drive probabilities and expected points from play-by-play data; GSE lifts no sportsbook lines, spreads, totals, or implied odds. The application makes the efficiency decomposition concrete. The 2010 Eagles scored fifty point six eight points above expectation on offense and prevented twenty-five point one nine on defense, with passing only slightly above average at plus eight point zero eight but rushing the league best at plus fifty-five point eight one thanks to Michael Vick; passing plus rushing NEP does not equal total NEP because aborted snaps and pre-snap penalties are separate play types that typically reduce scoring chance. The league table shows New England's offense at plus one hundred sixty-nine point seven three and Pittsburgh's defense at minus one hundred fifty-four point three zero, illustrating how the same expected-points scale grades both sides of the ball. The caveats close the account with the granularity and Markov limits. The distance binning that groups third-and-one with third-and-five is necessary for sample frequency but biases short-yardage conversion, so the probabilities and expected points should be adjusted for touchdowns, field goals, and punts; the Markov assumption ignores game-theoretic play-call history; and accuracy could be improved by separating late-game situations and adding more data. The invariant for GSE is to carry the absorbing-chain drive model, the absorption-probability and expected-points formulas, and the NEP play-value metric while recording the distance-binning bias, the play-call non-Markovian caveat, and the late-game-separation refinement before any quantitative reuse, treating expected points as a situational league-expectation benchmark rather than a team-specific truth. Two further structural points deserve emphasis. The fundamental matrix inverse of I minus Q is not merely an algebraic convenience: its entries are the expected number of visits to each transient state before absorption, so the same object simultaneously yields absorption probabilities when multiplied by R, expected drive length when its rows are summed, and expected points when weighted by scoring values, a single unifying computation GSE can reuse. The fourth-down absorption curves show the decision geography clearly: around the thirty-yard line the missed-field-goal and turnover-on-downs probabilities rise sharply while punt and field-goal probabilities move inversely, marking the zone where a coach must choose between punting, attempting a long field goal, or going for it. The deeper philosophy is that expected points turns every situation into a comparable currency, so a team's actual outcomes can be graded against the league expectation in that exact state, which is precisely the situational efficiency audit GSE performs.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: Founding absorbing-Markov drive model underlying modern EP. Keith Goldner, Northwestern; JQAS 2012 Manuscript 1400, DOI 10.1515/1559-0410.1400. EP lineage: Virgil Carter (Bengals 1971 Operations Research) -> Hidden Game (Carroll 1989) -> Burke/Schatz/Alamar (non-linear field-position EP). Motivating case: 2003 playoff 4th-and-26 own 25 (McNabb->Mitchell) -> FG 1/175. State=(down,distance,yardline); Markov property Eq1 (caveat: play-call game theory, run/pass not variables). Data 2005-2009 PBP ~200k plays/30k drives/1280 games (Lyu/AdvancedNFLStats, checked vs PFR). 20 zones (5yd)/distance 5-yd bins (>20 lumped); 340 transient + 9 absorbing = 349.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: 9 absorbing: TD/FG/safety/missed FG/fumble/INT/downs/punt/end-half. Transition P partitioned Q(340x340)/R(340x9)/0/I (Grinstead 1997). Absorption B=(I-Q)^-1 R (Eq5). Expected time t=(I-Q)^-1 c (Eq6, c=ones); 2nd-7 opp32 ~4.36 plays, max 7.57/min 1. EP=rho_TD*7+rho_FG*3+rho_SAF*(-2) (Eq7)=B x A; TD value 6.96 (96% XP). Empirical EP example 1.23, Markov 1.24 (1st-10 own20). EP curve: own goal line ~0.72, opp 1-yd ~6 (80.3% TD/12.6% FG). NEP=EP(n+1)-EP(n)+points (Alamar 2010). Equations printed readable text math, rendered LaTeX.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Validation: 1st-10 own20 FG 9.3% model vs 10.3% actual (avg dev 0.45%); 2nd-5 TD 30.0 vs 31.3 (0.78%); 3rd-1 TD 37.9 vs 45.1 (7.2%, avg 1.9%) — grouped w/ 3rd-5 coarse-bin bias (3rd-1 vs 3rd-5 avg dev 5.5%, punt 11.2/TD 10.9/FG 9.2); adjust TD/FG/punt. 1st-10 own20 punt 49.8%. 2010 Eagles off +50.68/def -25.19, pass +8.08/rush +55.81 (Vick league best); PNEP+RNEP != NEP (aborted snaps/penalties); run/pass same EP scale (passing more efficient). NE top off +169.73, PIT def -154.30. Future: separate late-game + more data. Markov ignores play-call history. Zero sportsbook lines lifted.

universal_lens: A foundational absorbing-Markov model represents a football drive as transitions among 349 down-distance-yardline states (340 transient, 9 absorbing drive-endings), computes absorption probabilities B=(I-Q)^-1 R and expected plays to absorption t=(I-Q)^-1 c from a 2005-2009 play-by-play transition matrix, and converts absorption probabilities into expected points EP=rho_TD*7+rho_FG*3+rho_SAF*(-2) (touchdown valued 6.96 for the extra point), with Net Expected Points measuring play efficiency as the expected-points delta plus points scored; it is validated against actual drive endings and honestly flags the short-yardage distance-binning bias and the play-call non-Markovian limitation.
gsi_mapping: GSI treats state=(down 1-4,distance 1-100,yardline 1-99); Markov Eq1 P(X_{n+1}|X_1..X_n)=P(X_{n+1}|X_n) (play-call game-theory caveat); 2005-2009 PBP ~200k plays/30k drives/1280 games; 20 five-yard zones + 5-yd distance bins (>20 lumped); 340 transient + 9 absorbing (TD/FG/safety/missed FG/fumble/INT/downs/punt/end-half)=349; P=[[Q,R],[0,I]]; B=(I-Q)^-1 R (Eq5); t=(I-Q)^-1 c (Eq6); EP=rho_TD*7+rho_FG*3+rho_SAF*(-2)=B x A (Eq7), TD 6.96 (96% XP); empirical EP 1.23/Markov 1.24; EP curve own goal line ~0.72/opp 1-yd ~6 (80.3% TD/12.6% FG); NEP=EP(n+1)-EP(n)+points (Alamar 2010); validation 1st-10 own20 FG 9.3 vs 10.3 (avg 0.45%), 3rd-1 TD 37.9 vs 45.1 (7.2% coarse-bin bias, 3rd-1 vs 3rd-5 dev 5.5%); 1st-10 own20 punt 49.8%; 2010 Eagles off +50.68/rush +55.81 (Vick), PNEP+RNEP != NEP, run/pass common scale; equations printed readable text math.
gse_mapping: GSE lifts the absorbing-chain drive-state model, the absorption-probability formula B=(I-Q)^-1 R, the expected-points formula EP=B x A, the expected-absorption-time drive-length estimate, and the NEP play-value metric as its drive-state, expected-points, and EPA layer; treats the distance-binning short-yardage bias as a granularity-correction requirement, the play-call game-theory caveat as a non-Markovian limitation, the common-scale run/pass comparison as an opportunity-cost baseline, and the late-game-separation plus more-data refinement as honest improvement paths; all outputs are drive probabilities and expected points from play-by-play data, never sportsbook lines, and expected points is a situational league-expectation benchmark rather than a team-specific truth.
